newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - London's crumbling tube a threat to city.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - London's crumbling tube a threat to city.

text.p: "It absolutely does my head in -- I'm late for work every morning and practically suffocated on the way. If I could cycle in a suit I'd never take the tube again," said an outraged commuter, venting her anger at yet another delay on London's notorious "tube".
Multiply her reaction by 780 million, the number of individual journeys made each year on London's Underground, and the scale of the problem becomes apparent.

London's continued role as a world financial and tourist centre is being undermined by its shaky underground rail system. Years of underfunding have culminated in a major cash crisis, passengers and pressure groups say.

The maze of tube lines beneath the capital creaks under the strain of 2.7 million passengers every day. Some of the rolling stock, track and signalling equipment dates back to the 1930s and is in desperate need of refurbishment.

But government cuts have resulted in delays and station closures running at their highest level for four years, according to 1996 figures from the Capital Transport Campaign, a London-wide transport pressure group.

"Denied the extra investment needed to reverse years of neglect and underfunding, London Underground is losing the battle to provide passengers with the decent service they deserve," said the Campaign's Andy Burns.

Their latest figures -- compiled from London Underground data -- showed the number of station closures nearly doubled in 1996, with 1,606 closed for more than 15 minutes. They also reported a four percent increase in major train delays.

Burns said the figures contradicted a recent statement by London's Transport Minister John Bowis that "under the government, underground services are improving". Burns said the remarks insulted passengers "who are being forced to endure an appalling service while ministers twiddle their thumbs".
GOVERNMENT SEES PRIVATISATION AS THE SOLUTION
On Tuesday, the Conservative government finally came up with what they see as a solution -- privatisation.

Just days after cuts in government funding caused London Transport to delay a number of big investment projects until the 21st century, Transport Secretary Sir George Young said the future of the Underground lay in the private sector.
State funding for the tube is due to fall from 950 million pounds ($1.5 billion) last year to 150 million by the year 2000.
The opposition Labour Party, hot favourites to win an election due by May 22, is firmly committed to keeping it in public hands but encourages private sector investment.
Burns said he was opposed to the privatisation, which could raise between 600 million and 1.5 billion pounds.
"I don't think it's the answer," he told Reuters, "In fact I think it could make the situation considerably worse."

He is concerned that funds would be diverted into shareholder dividends rather than being injected into improvements to the system. Privatisation could also lead to fragmentation of the network and cuts to off-peak and peripheral services.

Eleven tube lines connect the 267 underground stations -- some of which date back to 1865. Faced with disruption on a daily basis, commuters and tourists alike are losing their patience with the world's oldest underground system.

"I'm fed up with it," said human resources manager Janice Halford, caught up in severe overcrowding last week. "I travel on the tube every day and it's absolutely terrible. There are always cancellations and it's getting worse and worse."
Halford, who blamed the problem on incompetent management, said she had written six or seven letters of complaint but had yet to receive a satisfactory reply.
She had been on the platform for 15 minutes after two trains broke down on the main east-west line, and three stations were closed because of overcrowding and faulty escalators.
Tourists squashed by crowds of commuters leaving work said they were scared of being pushed onto the line.
"It's really daunting when it's this crowded," said a 24-year-old Irish tourist. "I think the fares are outrageous too, considering it's so busy and dirty."
"I hate the London Underground," said a Polish student, "the delays are much worse than in Paris or St Petersburg...I try not to use it on Saturdays because it's so crowded it's dangerous."
OVERCROWDING TO GET WORSE
And the overcrowding is set to worsen. Experts say London's economy will grow more rapidly than Britain's in the future. Within 20 years, the number of passengers could rise by 20 percent.

The few stations lucky enough to have been refurbished have improved dramatically, but years of inadequate investment have left a backlog of work which would cost 1.25 billion pounds ($2 billion), according to the Confederation of British Industry.

The Northern line, one of the oldest and most rickety, suffers from so much disruption that Londoners call it the 'misery line'. Defective trains, signal failures and track defects contributed to its 389 incidents reported in 1996.
"It's certainly a misery line at the weekend," said retired insurance salesman George Sayers. "It's a very scruffy line and you can never rely on getting anywhere on time."
A breakdown in a 91-year-old power station last November left 30,000 passengers stranded in tunnels and stations, and brought the entire network to a halt for more than two hours.
Crowds of bewildered tourists and angry locals spilled into the bitterly cold streets, faced with endless taxi queues and dangerously overcrowded buses -- or a long walk home.

An even more serious power cut in April trapped tens of thousands of people and left 31 needing hospital treatment for smoke inhalation. With 10 to 15 million people expected to pour into London for the Millennium celebrations, pressure is mounting for immediate action before the system quite literally crumbles.
